Structural and electrochemical behaviour of bilayer manganite LaSr2Mn2O6.96 cathode for all-solid-state fluoride ion batteries
abstract: In this study, we explore the potential of the RP-type bilayer manganite LaSr2Mn2O6.96 as an intercalation-based cathode material for all-solid-state fluoride ion batteries (FIBs). Structural changes of LaSr2Mn2O6.96 during fluoride intercalation and de-intercalation were analyzed via ex-situ X-ray diffraction, revealing that F- insertion induces the formation of three distinct tetragonal phases. To understand the complex behavior of these phases, we examined the changes in the Mn oxidation state and coordination environment using X-ray absorption spectroscopy and magnetic measurements. Under stack pressure (20 kN), electrochemical cycling of LaSr2Mn2O6.96 in the potential range of 1 V to -1 V exhibited a continuous increase in specific capacity from capacity of ~ 30 mAh/g to ~ 68 mAh/g over 200 cycles, with ~99 % coulombic efficiency and no signs of capacity fading. This makes the bilayer manganite LaSr2Mn2O6.96 a promising candidate for a cycling stable cathode for all-solid-state FIBs, especially under the application of stack pressure.

title: Ionic polarization engineering of polymeric carbon nitride toward efficient H2O2 photosynthesis
Unlocking the performance of sodium-ion batteries by coating Na3V2(PO4)3 with Nb2O5
abstract: Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 (NVP) is a promising cathode material for sodium-ion batteries owing to its NASICON-type framework, which enables efficient reversible sodium insertion. However, its practical performance is limited by slow charge transfer at high cycling rates and cycling instability. Here, we report a facile impregnation method to deposit Nb 2 O 5 on NVP particles, aiming to enhance high-rate capability and long-term cycling stability. Structural and spectroscopic analyses (XRD, electron microscopy, Raman, XPS, and X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy) confirm the crystallinity of NVP and the uniform presence of Nb 2 O 5 on particle surfaces without compromising sodium reversibility. Electrochemical measurements reveal that Nb 2 O 5 -coated samples show the highest diffusion coefficients, ensuring superior high-rate performance and cycling stability. The 3% Nb 2 O 5 coating delivers the highest diffusion coefficients, superior cycling stability, and sustained capacity retention at a 1C rate. Cyclic voltammetry and impedance spectroscopy indicate enhanced surface capacitance, facilitating rapid sodium storage. XPS shows the conversion of Nb 2 O 5 into NbF 5 , resulting from HF scavenging, which improved interfacial stability. Extended cycling tests validate the long-term durability of the coated electrode. These results demonstrate that Nb 2 O 5 surface modification is an effective strategy to overcome the intrinsic limitations of NVP, offering a viable route to high-performance sodium-ion batteries.

T2MAT (text-to-material): A universal agent for generating material structures with goal properties from a single sentence
abstract: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC)-content autonomously produced by AI systems without human intervention-has significantly boosted efficiency across various fields. However, AIGC in material science faces challenges in efficiently discovering novel materials that surpass existing databases, while simultaneously addressing the invariance and stability of crystal structures. To address these challenges, we develop T2MAT (text-to-material), a comprehensive agent processing from a user-input sentence to inverse design material structures with goal properties beyond the existing database via globally exploring chemical space, followed by an entirely automated workflow of first-principles validation. Furthermore, we propose CGTNet (Crystal Graph Transformer NETwork), a graph neural network model that captures long-range interactions, to enhance the accuracy and data utilization efficiency of property prediction and thereby strengthen the reliability of inverse design. Through these contributions, T2MAT minimizes the dependency on human expertise and significantly improves the efficiency of discovering novel, high-performance functional materials, offering a robust way toward more autonomous materials design.

Electrochemical-driven structural engineering of highly oxidized carbon nitride nanosheets for tuneable photocatalytic performance
abstract: Carbon nitride is a promising metal-free semiconductor for photocatalytic applications; however, conventional thermal routes often provide limited control over its structural order and surface chemistry. In this work, a galvanostatic electrochemical strategy is presented for the synthesis of hydroxyl-functionalized carbon nitride quantum dot-like species (OH-C3N4-QDs), which act as tuneable precursors for oxygen-rich carbon nitride nanosheets (CNO) obtained after acid treatment. By systematically varying the applied current density, materials with different degrees of condensation, oxidation and surface nitrogen enrichment were produced. Structural and compositional evolution of the resulting CNO nanosheets was investigated by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Raman spectroscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Transmission Electron microscopy (TEM), UV-Vis spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), revealing the formation of ordered CN intermediate phases and controlled incorporation of oxygen functionalities. The electrochemical parameters were shown to govern stacking coherence, interlayer interactions and surface chemical environments. The photocatalytic behaviour was evaluated using Rhodamine B degradation under simulated solar irradiation. Compared with the OH-C3N4-QDs precursor, the oxidized nanosheets exhibit enhanced photocatalytic activity, which correlates with surface nitrogen enrichment and moderate oxidation rather than with surface area or band gap values. These results demonstrate that electrochemical synthesis provides an effective route for tailoring the structure and surface chemistry of carbon nitride materials, establishing clear structure–activity relationships relevant to photocatalytic processes.

Suppressing nonradiative energy loss in organic solar cells with 20.79% efficiency via thiophene-terminal engineering of a twisted acceptor
abstract: Minimizing nonradiative energy loss (ΔEnr) is a critical imperative for bridging the efficiency gap in organic solar cells (OSCs). Herein, we demonstrate a thiophene-terminal engineering strategy to develop a twisted small-molecule acceptor, named as AQx-2T. By substituting conventional terminal groups with electron-donating thiophene moieties, the intramolecular charge-transfer character is effectively moderated, leading to upshifted frontier molecular orbitals and a high open-circuit voltage (VOC) exceeding 1.0 V in D18:AQx-2T binary devices. Crucially, the rotational freedom of the thiophene linkages induces a more twisted molecular conformation, which successfully mitigates excessive aggregation and reduces crystallinity. Consequently, AQx-2T achieves an ultralow ΔEnr of 0.182 eV. When introduced as a guest acceptor into the highly crystalline D18:L8-BO host matrix, AQx-2T promotes acceptor co-assembly, moderates molecular ordering, suppresses large-scale phase separation, and refines the bulk-heterojunction morphology. Benefiting from improved exciton dissociation, balanced charge transport, and minimized recombination, the optimized ternary D18:L8-BO:AQx-2T device achieves an outstanding power conversion efficiency of 20.79%, accompanied by a reduced ΔEnr from 0.216 eV to 0.197 eV. This work demonstrates that balancing molecular planarity and electronic structures via terminal engineering provides a powerful paradigm for overcoming the voltage deficit in high-performance OSCs.

Progress and perspectives of molten salt batteries
abstract: Rechargeable molten-salt batteries represent a promising technology for large-scale energy storage, offering intrinsic safety, high power density, and low cost. Unlike flammable organic liquid electrolytes with limited thermal stability and ionic conductivity, molten-salt electrolytes are nonflammable and highly conductive, making them an attractive alternative. However, challenges such as limited energy density, capacity degradation, and parasitic side reactions (e.g., corrosion) remain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the historical development of molten-salt batteries, emphasizing representative chemistries including thermal primary cells, Na-S, Na-NiCl 2 , liquid metal, metal-air, low-temperature Al-based, and dual-intercalation systems. We highlight the evolution in four distinct configurations, high-temperature cells with solid ion conductors (i.e., ceramic), liquid metal batteries, solid-electrode systems with low-melting-point electrolytes, and metal-air designs, that offer diverse performance trade-offs, from high-energy-density Li-metal cells (∼400 Wh kg −1 ) to ultra-low-cost Fe-air systems (<100 $ kWh −1 ). Despite persistent challenges such as high viscosity, poor wettability, and the need for scalable thermal management and durable components, low-melting-point molten salts provide safer alternatives to flammable organics. Liquid metal batteries show particular promise for grid-scale storage, while molten-salt metal-CO 2 cells uniquely couple energy storage with carbon utilization. Overcoming these interdisciplinary hurdles positions molten-salt batteries to become suitable technologies for resilient, renewable-powered energy grids. Rechargeable molten-salt batteries represent a promising technology for large-scale energy storage, offering intrinsic safety, high power density, and low cost, with their key advantage lying in molten-salt electrolytes that are nonflammable and highly conductive; unlike flammable organic liquid electrolytes with limited thermal stability and ionic conductivity, molten salts avoid volatile solvents, reducing fire and explosion risks while enabling fast charge and discharge, and many can be made from abundant, inexpensive materials, making them attractive for grid-scale storage where safety, cost, and longevity matter. However, challenges remain, including limited energy density, capacity degradation, and parasitic side reactions such as corrosion, and corrosion of current collectors, seals, and housings, along with electrode dissolution and unwanted interfacial reactions, shortens cycle life and lowers efficiency, while high operating temperatures can accelerate degradation and require robust thermal management, insulation, and hermetic sealing, and freeze-thaw cycling, material compatibility, and durable components further complicate deployment. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the historical development of molten-salt batteries, emphasizing representative chemistries including thermal primary cells, Na-S, Na-NiCl 2 , liquid metal, metal-air, low-temperature Al-based, and dual-intercalation systems; early thermal primary cells, such as Li-FeS 2 reserve batteries, proved molten-salt electrolytes could work in harsh conditions, though they were not rechargeable, while Na-S batteries offered high energy density and low-cost materials but required high temperatures and faced safety and sealing issues, Na-NiCl 2 or ZEBRA batteries improved safety and enabled moderate-temperature operation, liquid metal batteries introduced all-liquid electrodes and electrolytes, supporting high current density and long life for stationary storage, metal-air systems, especially Fe-air, promise ultra-low cost but suffer from low round-trip efficiency and air-electrode challenges, and low-temperature Al-based and dual-intercalation systems expand the design space by reducing operating temperatures and exploring multivalent or dual-ion chemistries. We highlight the evolution in four distinct configurations, including high-temperature cells with solid ion conductors (i.e., ceramic), liquid metal batteries, solid-electrode systems with low-melting-point electrolytes, and metal-air designs. These configurations offer diverse performance trade-offs, from high-energy-density Li-metal cells (∼400 Wh kg −1 ) to ultra-low-cost Fe-air systems (<100 $ kWh −1 ), and each balances energy density, power density, cycle life, safety, and cost differently, making molten-salt batteries suitable for differentiated niches rather than one universal application. Despite persistent challenges such as high viscosity, poor wettability, and the need for scalable thermal management and durable components, low-melting-point molten salts provide safer alternatives to flammable organics. Liquid metal batteries show particular promise for grid-scale storage, while molten-salt metal-CO 2 cells uniquely couple energy storage with carbon utilization, and overcoming these interdisciplinary hurdles, spanning materials science, electrochemistry, thermal engineering, and system integration, positions molten-salt batteries to become suitable technologies for resilient, renewable-powered energy grids, so that by addressing these challenges they are well positioned to transition from compelling laboratory prototypes to cornerstone technologies, occupying differentiated niches that range from bulk, low-cost storage to high-performance, high-value applications.
